Assignment 2B — RAG Pipeline (Manufacturing & Technical Standards)¶

Course: Large Language Models for Generative AI (S1-26_AIMLZG536) Group: 78

Builds a small, complete Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system on the Assignment 1 domain corpus:

12 cleaned .txt docs ──► chunk ──► embed ──► FAISS (dense) ─┐
                              └──► BM25 (keyword) ──────────┼─► RRF hybrid ─► cross-encoder rerank ─► top-3 chunks
                                                                                                         │
                         Assignment 1 model (TinyLlama-1.1B + QLoRA Adapter B) ◄── grounded prompt ◄──────┘
                                         │
                                         └──► LLM judge (correct? supported?)
Part What we do Marks
A Dense search + choose a chunk size 5
B Dense vs BM25 vs Hybrid (RRF) 4
C Cross-encoder reranking 4
D Grounded generation + LLM judge 7

Reused from Assignment 1: the 12 cleaned domain .txt files, the 10-pair evaluation set (eval_dataset.jsonl, seed-42 split), and the fine-tuned TinyLlama-1.1B + QLoRA Adapter B.

Models actually used in Part D: the Assignment 1 model ignored the chunks (no citations, no "Not found"), so — as the brief allows — the final answers come from microsoft/Phi-3.5-mini-instruct; the judge is Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

Step 0 — Environment setup¶

Parts A–C run on CPU or GPU. Part D loads LLMs and needs a GPU (Prayogshala / Colab).

0.1 Load the document collection¶

We reuse the cleaned Assignment 1 files as-is. Only whitespace is collapsed — we deliberately do not fix the OCR noise (e.g. management-ied, weii) because real RAG systems must cope with imperfect text, and the answer spans below are copied verbatim from this text.

In [10]:
def normalize_ws(text: str) -> str:
    # Collapse all runs of whitespace (newlines, tabs, double spaces) to a single space.
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()

docs = {p.name: normalize_ws(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore"))
        for p in sorted(CORPUS_DIR.glob("*.txt"))}

corpus_stats = pd.DataFrame([{"document": n, "characters": len(t), "words": len(t.split())} for n, t in docs.items()])
print(f"{len(docs)} documents | {corpus_stats.characters.sum():,} characters | {corpus_stats.words.sum():,} words")

0.2 The 10 evaluation queries and their answer spans¶

The queries and expected answers are the 10-pair evaluation split from Assignment 1 (48 curated pairs, 80/20 split, random.seed(42)).

Answer span = the sentence or short passage in the corpus that answers the query. A retrieved chunk is a hit if it contains the span. Each span was found by searching the query's source document and copied verbatim (OCR errors included). Spans are kept short (13–27 tokens) so that each one can fit inside even a 100-token chunk.

# Hit test used in Parts A, B and C: case- and whitespace-insensitive substring match
def norm(s: str) -> str:
    return normalize_ws(s).lower()

def is_hit(chunk_text: str, span: str) -> bool:
    return norm(span) in norm(chunk_text)

# Sanity check: every span must exist (exactly once) in its source document
for e in EVAL:
    n = norm(docs[e["source"]]).count(norm(e["span"]))
    assert n >= 1, f"Q{e['qid']}: span not found in {e['source']}"
    e["span_occurrences"] = n

Part A — Dense search and chunk size (5 marks)¶

Dense retrieval in one paragraph. An embedding model maps any text to a fixed-length vector so that texts with similar meaning land close together. We embed every chunk once (offline), store the vectors in an index, and at query time embed the query and return the chunks whose vectors are most similar. If all vectors are L2-normalised, the inner product equals cosine similarity, so a FAISS IndexFlatIP (exact, brute-force inner-product search) gives exact cosine-similarity search.

Embedding model choice and its input limit¶

The assignment asks for chunk sizes of 100 and 400 tokens. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 truncates input at 256 tokens, so a 400-token chunk would lose its last ~144 tokens when embedded (they would still be sent to the LLM, but would be invisible to search). We therefore switched to a model with a longer limit: BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 — 512-token limit, 384-dim vectors, 33M parameters, so it is just as cheap to run. Tokens are counted with this model's own tokenizer.

BGE models are trained with an instruction prefix for short queries ("Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: "); passages are embedded without it.

In [12]:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import faiss

EMBED_MODEL_ID = "BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5"
QUERY_PREFIX   = "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: "
EMBED_BATCH    = 64

embedder  = SentenceTransformer(EMBED_MODEL_ID, device=DEVICE)
tokenizer = embedder.tokenizer
MAX_TOKENS = embedder.max_seq_length            # limit applied when embedding (incl. [CLS]/[SEP])
EMBED_DIM  = (embedder.get_embedding_dimension() if hasattr(embedder, "get_embedding_dimension")
              else embedder.get_sentence_embedding_dimension())

print("Embedding model :", EMBED_MODEL_ID)
print("Max input length:", MAX_TOKENS, "tokens")
print("Vector size     :", EMBED_DIM)

def count_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    return len(tokenizer(text, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"])

A1. Build dense search (2 marks)¶

A1.1 — One reusable dense-search component¶

DenseIndex embeds a list of chunks, builds a FAISS IndexFlatIP, and search(query, k) returns the top-k chunks with scores. The same class is reused for every chunk size in A2 and again in Parts B and C.

In [13]:
class DenseIndex:
    # Embed chunks -> FAISS IndexFlatIP (cosine via normalised vectors) -> top-k search.

    def __init__(self, chunks, model=embedder, batch_size=EMBED_BATCH, query_prefix=QUERY_PREFIX):
        self.chunks, self.model, self.batch_size, self.query_prefix = chunks, model, batch_size, query_prefix
        texts = [c["text"] for c in chunks]

        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        vecs = model.encode(texts, batch_size=batch_size, normalize_embeddings=True,
                            convert_to_numpy=True, show_progress_bar=False).astype("float32")
        t1 = time.perf_counter()
        self.index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(vecs.shape[1])
        self.index.add(vecs)
        t2 = time.perf_counter()

        self.embed_seconds, self.add_seconds = t1 - t0, t2 - t1
        self.build_seconds = t2 - t0

    def search(self, query: str, k: int = 5):
        q = self.model.encode([self.query_prefix + query], normalize_embeddings=True,
                              convert_to_numpy=True).astype("float32")
        scores, ids = self.index.search(q, k)
        return [{**self.chunks[i], "score": float(s), "rank": r}
                for r, (i, s) in enumerate(zip(ids[0], scores[0]), start=1)]

A2. Choose a chunk size (3 marks)¶

Fixed-size chunking with the embedding model's tokenizer¶

Each document is tokenized once with return_offsets_mapping=True. That gives, for every token, its character position in the original text, so a window of N tokens can be cut directly from the original text (no decode step, so casing and punctuation are preserved). Chunks never cross document boundaries, and there is no overlap, as the assignment specifies.

Both sizes fit the model: 100 + 2 and 400 + 2 special tokens are ≤ 512, so nothing is truncated.

In [14]:
def chunk_fixed(docs: dict, size: int):
    # Split every document into consecutive, non-overlapping windows of `size` tokens.
    chunks = []
    for name, text in docs.items():
        enc = tokenizer(text, add_special_tokens=False, return_offsets_mapping=True, verbose=False)
        offsets = enc["offset_mapping"]
        for start in range(0, len(offsets), size):
            window = offsets[start:start + size]
            chunks.append({
                "chunk_id": len(chunks),
                "doc": name,
                "text": text[window[0][0]:window[-1][1]],
                "n_tokens": len(window),
            })
    return chunks

CHUNK_SIZES = [100, 400]
chunk_sets = {size: chunk_fixed(docs, size) for size in CHUNK_SIZES}

for size, chunks in chunk_sets.items():
    assert max(c["n_tokens"] for c in chunks) + 2 <= MAX_TOKENS
    print(f"{size:>3}-token chunks: {len(chunks):>5} chunks | example from {chunks[1]['doc']}:")
    print(textwrap.indent(textwrap.fill(chunks[1]["text"][:300] + " ...", 110), "    "))

Can every span be found at each size? With no overlap, a span that happens to straddle a chunk boundary is split in two, and no chunk can ever contain it. Checking this up front tells us the best hit rate each chunk size could possibly reach.

A2.1 — Dense search at 100 vs 400 tokens (2 marks)¶

For each size: build the dense index (A1), retrieve the top 3 for each of the 10 queries, and compute

  • Hit rate@3 — share of queries where one of the top-3 chunks contains the answer span
  • Tokens sent per query — combined token count of the top-3 chunks, averaged over the 10 queries
In [16]:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

# The generator (Assignment 1 TinyLlama) uses a different tokenizer from the embedder, so count its tokens too
GEN_MODEL_ID  = "TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0"
gen_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(GEN_MODEL_ID)

def count_gen_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    return len(gen_tokenizer(text, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"])

def hit_at_k(results, span, k):
    return any(is_hit(r["text"], span) for r in results[:k])

dense_indexes, a2_rows, a2_detail = {}, [], []
for size, chunks in chunk_sets.items():
    idx = DenseIndex(chunks)
    dense_indexes[size] = idx
    hits, tokens_sent, gen_tokens_sent = [], [], []
    for e in EVAL:
        top3 = idx.search(e["query"], k=3)
        hit_rank = next((r["rank"] for r in top3 if is_hit(r["text"], e["span"])), None)
        hits.append(hit_rank is not None)
        tokens_sent.append(sum(r["n_tokens"] for r in top3))
        gen_tokens_sent.append(sum(count_gen_tokens(r["text"]) for r in top3))
        a2_detail.append({"chunk size": size, "qid": e["qid"], "hit rank (top 3)": hit_rank or "-",
                          "top-1 doc": top3[0]["doc"], "correct doc": e["source"]})
    a2_rows.append({"Chunk size (tokens)": size,
                    "Total chunks": len(chunks),
                    "Hit rate@3 (%)": 100 * np.mean(hits),
                    "Tokens sent per query (top 3)": round(np.mean(tokens_sent), 1),
                    "TinyLlama tokens per query (avg)": round(np.mean(gen_tokens_sent), 1),
                    "TinyLlama tokens per query (max)": max(gen_tokens_sent),
                    "Index build time (s)": round(idx.build_seconds, 2)})

a2_table = pd.DataFrame(a2_rows)
a2_table

Observations from the A2 results

  • Same hit rate@3 (60%), different queries. 100-token chunks hit Q1, Q3, Q4, Q6, Q8, Q9; 400-token chunks hit Q2, Q3, Q6, Q7, Q8, Q9. Q2 is only reachable at 400 (its span is split at 100); Q7 needs the longer window.
  • Rank 1 is better with small chunks — 3/10 at 100 tokens (Q6, Q8, Q9) vs 0/10 at 400. A small chunk's embedding is dominated by the answer sentence; a 400-token chunk mixes several topics, so its vector is "diluted" and lands at rank 2–3.
  • Right document, wrong passage. Q5 and Q10 are missed at both sizes, yet the top-1 chunk comes from the correct document for 10/10 queries at 100 tokens and 9/10 at 400. Dense search finds the right area; the problem is ranking within it — exactly what hybrid search (Part B) and reranking (Part C) target.
  • Build time is about equal (12.5 s vs 13.5 s) even though 100-token chunks are 4× more numerous: the total number of tokens embedded is the same (~640k), only packed into more, shorter sequences.
  • Tokenizers differ. One BGE token ≈ 1.25 TinyLlama tokens on this corpus (OCR noise and numbers split into many pieces), so "1,200 tokens" for the embedder is ~1,500 for the generator.

A2.2 — Chosen chunk size (1 mark)¶

We use 400-token chunks for Parts B–D. Both sizes reach the same hit rate@3 (60%), but at 100 tokens the answer spans of Q2 and Q5 are cut across chunk boundaries, capping that size at 80%, while every span stays intact at 400 tokens and each chunk carries enough surrounding text for multi-part answers. The cost is 4× more context — about 1,200 embedding tokens (≈1,500 TinyLlama tokens) per query — which still fits TinyLlama's 2,048-token window next to a short prompt and a ~250-token answer; unusually long OCR-heavy chunks are trimmed by a token budget in Part D, and the weaker rank-1 accuracy of large chunks (0/10 vs 3/10) is what reranking in Part C should recover.

Observation: almost all of the build time is spent embedding the chunks (a forward pass of the model per chunk); adding vectors to a flat FAISS index is just a memory copy. The flat index is exact; at this corpus size (a few thousand vectors) approximate indexes such as HNSW or IVF are unnecessary.

Part B — Keyword and hybrid search (4 marks)¶

All three methods search the same 1,601 × 400-token chunks, return the top 5, and are scored on the same 10 queries.

Method Matches on Strong when Weak when
Dense (BGE + FAISS) meaning (vectors) the query paraphrases the text ("awkward posture" ≈ "bending and reaching") exact names, numbers, codes; diluted long chunks
BM25 (keywords) exact word overlap, weighted by rarity rare, specific terms ("Type A", "ISO 9002", "cascading") synonyms, paraphrases, OCR-mangled words
Hybrid (RRF) ranks from both lists the two methods make different mistakes both methods miss the same chunk

Shared evaluation harness¶

evaluate() runs one warm-up query (not timed), then times each of the 10 queries end-to-end (query in → top 5 out) and records the rank of the first chunk that contains the answer span.

In [20]:
TOP_K = 5

def first_hit_rank(results, span):
    return next((r["rank"] for r in results if is_hit(r["text"], span)), None)

def evaluate(search_fn, k=TOP_K):
    search_fn(QUERIES[0], k)                                   # warm-up run, not timed
    per_query, latencies = [], []
    for e in EVAL:
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        results = search_fn(e["query"], k)
        latencies.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000)
        per_query.append({"qid": e["qid"], "hit_rank": first_hit_rank(results, e["span"]), "results": results})
    ranks = [p["hit_rank"] for p in per_query]
    pct = lambda flags: round(100 * float(np.mean(flags)), 1)
    summary = {"Average query latency (ms)": round(float(np.mean(latencies)), 2),
               "Hit rate@1 (%)": pct([r == 1 for r in ranks]),
               "Hit rate@3 (%)": pct([r is not None and r <= 3 for r in ranks]),
               "Hit rate@5 (%)": pct([r is not None for r in ranks])}
    return summary, per_query

b_summary, b_per_query = {}, {}

B2. BM25 (1 mark)¶

BM25 scores a chunk by summing, over each query word, how rare the word is (IDF) × how often it appears in the chunk (TF), with two corrections:

  • TF saturation (k1 = 1.5) — the 10th "maintenance" in a chunk adds far less than the 1st.
  • Length normalisation (b = 0.75) — long chunks are penalised for containing more words by chance.

Tokenisation: lowercase, split on non-alphanumerics (so ISO 9001 → iso, 9001), and drop common English stopwords, which carry no topical signal. Note that OCR damage hurts BM25 directly: management-ied becomes management + ied, and led will never match it.

In [22]:
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi

STOPWORDS = set("""a an and are as at be been being but by can could did do does for from had has have how i if in into is
it its may might must not of on or our should so such than that the their them then there these they this those to was
we were what when where which while who why will with would you your""".split())

def bm25_tokenize(text: str):
    return [t for t in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower()) if t not in STOPWORDS]

class BM25Index:
    def __init__(self, chunks, k1=1.5, b=0.75):
        self.chunks = chunks
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        self.bm25 = BM25Okapi([bm25_tokenize(c["text"]) for c in chunks], k1=k1, b=b)
        self.build_seconds = time.perf_counter() - t0

    def search(self, query: str, k: int = TOP_K):
        scores = self.bm25.get_scores(bm25_tokenize(query))
        top = np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
        return [{**self.chunks[i], "score": float(scores[i]), "rank": r} for r, i in enumerate(top, start=1)]

bm25 = BM25Index(CHUNKS)
print(f"BM25 index built over {len(CHUNKS):,} chunks in {bm25.build_seconds:.2f} s")
print("Query tokens for Q8:", bm25_tokenize(EVAL[7]["query"]))

def bm25_search(query, k=TOP_K):
    return bm25.search(query, k)

b_summary["BM25"], b_per_query["BM25"] = evaluate(bm25_search)
b_summary["BM25"]

B3. Hybrid with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (1 mark)¶

Dense scores (cosine, ~0.5–0.9) and BM25 scores (unbounded, ~5–40) are on different scales, so adding them is meaningless. RRF uses only ranks:

$$\text{RRF}(d) = \frac{1}{60 + \text{rank}_\text{dense}(d)} + \frac{1}{60 + \text{rank}_\text{BM25}(d)}$$

We fuse the top 20 of each list (a chunk missing from a list gets 0 from it) and keep the top 5. The constant 60 flattens the curve: rank 1 is worth 1/61 ≈ 0.0164 and rank 20 still 1/80 = 0.0125, so a chunk ranked fairly well by both methods (e.g. 4th and 6th → 0.0156 + 0.0152 = 0.0308) beats a chunk ranked 1st by only one (0.0164).

In [23]:
RRF_K, FUSE_DEPTH = 60, 20

def rrf_fuse(ranked_lists: dict, k=TOP_K, rrf_k=RRF_K):
    # ranked_lists: {"dense": [...], "bm25": [...]}, each a list of results with 1-based "rank"
    fused = {}
    for method, results in ranked_lists.items():
        for r in results:
            entry = fused.setdefault(r["chunk_id"], {**r, "score": 0.0, "dense_rank": None, "bm25_rank": None})
            entry["score"] += 1.0 / (rrf_k + r["rank"])
            entry[f"{method}_rank"] = r["rank"]
    best = sorted(fused.values(), key=lambda x: x["score"], reverse=True)[:k]
    return [{**r, "rank": i} for i, r in enumerate(best, start=1)]

def hybrid_search(query, k=TOP_K):
    return rrf_fuse({"dense": dense.search(query, FUSE_DEPTH), "bm25": bm25.search(query, FUSE_DEPTH)}, k)

b_summary["Hybrid (RRF)"], b_per_query["Hybrid (RRF)"] = evaluate(hybrid_search)

# Worked example: where did the fused top 5 come from?
e = EVAL[2]   # Q3: dense rank 2, BM25 rank 5 -> fused rank 1
print(f"Q{e['qid']}: {e['query']}\n")
pd.DataFrame([{"fused rank": r["rank"], "RRF score": round(r["score"], 4), "dense rank": r["dense_rank"],
               "BM25 rank": r["bm25_rank"], "doc": r["doc"], "contains span": is_hit(r["text"], e["span"])}
              for r in hybrid_search(e["query"])])

Observations from the Part B results

  • Hybrid gives the best rank 1: hit@1 is 20% (Q3, Q9), vs 0% for dense and 10% for BM25, with the same hit@3 (60%) and hit@5 (70%) as dense.
  • The two methods fail on different queries, which is what RRF needs. BM25 wins where the query shares rare exact words with the passage (Q1 "Malcolm Baldrige … STEP" rank 2 vs dense 5; Q9 "management … quality improvement" rank 1 vs dense 3). Dense wins on paraphrases (Q2 "reaching / posture" vs the text's "diverters … reduces reaches", Q6 "costs" — BM25 misses both).
  • Agreement beats a single first place. Q3 is ranked 2nd by dense and 5th by BM25; neither puts it first, but it is the only chunk both rank highly, so RRF puts it at rank 1 (1/62 + 1/65 = 0.0315).
  • Fusion can also cost a little: Q2 drops from dense rank 3 to hybrid rank 4, because BM25 contributes nothing for it while other chunks collect points from both lists.
  • BM25 is weakest overall (30% hit@3) — the corpus is OCR text and the questions are paraphrased, so exact word overlap is low.
  • Q4, Q5, Q10 are missed by all three methods in the top 5. For Q5, every top result comes from the correct maintenance report but from summary sections that mention reactive maintenance many times, not from the definition passage.
  • Latency: BM25 is fastest (3 ms, no neural network). Dense takes ~11 ms, dominated by embedding the query on the GPU; hybrid (~14 ms) is roughly dense + BM25, since fusing two short lists costs almost nothing. Millisecond timings on a shared Colab GPU vary between runs, but all three are negligible next to LLM generation (seconds).

B4. Which method works best, and why (1 mark)¶

Hybrid (RRF) works best for our queries: it has the highest hit@1 (20% vs 0% dense, 10% BM25), the same hit@3 as dense (60%), for only ~3 ms more than dense (14 vs 11 ms; both are dominated by embedding the query). Dense and BM25 make different mistakes — dense matches meaning but ranks long, mixed-topic chunks loosely, while BM25 rewards exact technical terms but misses paraphrases — so fusing their ranks promotes chunks that both consider relevant. For example, for Q3 ("What three kinds of evidence can be used to assess results…") dense ranked the answer chunk 2nd and BM25 5th, but because it was the only chunk high in both lists, RRF moved it to rank 1.

Part C — Reranking (4 marks)¶

Why rerank? Dense search is a bi-encoder: the query and each chunk are embedded separately, and similarity is one dot product. That is fast enough to search thousands of chunks, but the chunk vector was computed without knowing the question, so a 400-token chunk is compressed into one "average" meaning. A cross-encoder reads the query and the chunk together in one transformer pass, so every query word can attend to every chunk word, and outputs a single relevance score. It is much more accurate but needs one forward pass per (query, chunk) pair, so it is only used on a short candidate list:

1,601 chunks ──hybrid (fast, recall)──► top 10 ──cross-encoder (slow, precision)──► top 3 ──► LLM

Model: cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 (6-layer MiniLM, trained on MS MARCO question → passage relevance). Its input limit is 512 tokens; a query (~25 tokens) + a 400-token chunk + 3 special tokens fits, so nothing is truncated (both models use the same uncased BERT WordPiece vocabulary).

Important limit: a reranker can only reorder the candidates it receives. If the answer chunk is not in the hybrid top 10, no reranker can recover it, so we first measure hit@10 as the ceiling.

In [27]:
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

RERANK_MODEL_ID = "cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2"
CANDIDATES_K, FINAL_K = 10, 3

reranker = CrossEncoder(RERANK_MODEL_ID, max_length=512, device=DEVICE)
print("Reranker:", RERANK_MODEL_ID, "| max length:", getattr(reranker, "max_seq_length", 512), "| device:", DEVICE)

# Ceiling check: in how many queries is the answer chunk among the 10 hybrid candidates?
candidates = {e["qid"]: hybrid_search(e["query"], CANDIDATES_K) for e in EVAL}
hit10 = [first_hit_rank(candidates[e["qid"]], e["span"]) for e in EVAL]
print(f"Hybrid hit@10 (best any reranker could reach for hit@1/hit@3): {100 * np.mean([r is not None for r in hit10]):.0f}%")
print("Rank of answer chunk in the hybrid top 10:", {f"Q{e['qid']}": r or "-" for e, r in zip(EVAL, hit10)})

C1. Rerank the hybrid top 10 and keep the top 3 (1 mark)¶

rerank() scores every (query, chunk) pair with the cross-encoder, sorts by that score and keeps the top 3. Only the cross-encoder step is timed (one warm-up call first), since the retrieval cost was already measured in Part B.

In [28]:
def rerank(query, cands, top_n=FINAL_K):
    scores = reranker.predict([(query, c["text"]) for c in cands], batch_size=16, show_progress_bar=False)
    order = np.argsort(-scores)
    return [{**cands[i], "hybrid_rank": cands[i]["rank"], "ce_score": float(scores[i]), "rank": new_rank}
            for new_rank, i in enumerate(order[:top_n], start=1)]

rerank(EVAL[0]["query"], candidates[1])                       # warm-up, not timed

reranked, rerank_ms = {}, []
for e in EVAL:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    reranked[e["qid"]] = rerank(e["query"], candidates[e["qid"]])
    rerank_ms.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000)

print(f"Reranked {len(EVAL)} queries | {CANDIDATES_K} candidates each | avg {np.mean(rerank_ms):.1f} ms per query")

def show_rerank(qid, width=200):
    # Readable before/after view of one query's top 3, with the start of each chunk's text.
    e = EVAL[qid - 1]
    print(f"Q{qid}: {e['query']}\nSpan: {e['span']}\n")
    for label, results in [("BEFORE (hybrid)", candidates[qid][:FINAL_K]), ("AFTER (cross-encoder)", reranked[qid])]:
        print(f"── {label} " + "─" * 50)
        for r in results:
            flag = "HIT " if is_hit(r["text"], e["span"]) else "    "
            extra = f" (was hybrid #{r['hybrid_rank']}, score {r['ce_score']:.2f})" if "ce_score" in r else ""
            print(f" {flag}#{r['rank']}{extra} [{r['doc']}] {r['text'][:width]}...")
        print()

for e in EVAL:

Observations from the reranking results

Query Answer-span rank, hybrid → reranked What happened
Q6 2 → 1 gain: the cost-definition chunk moved to the top
Q2 4 → 2 gain: pulled up from outside the top 3
Q9 1 → 3 loss on the metric, but the new #2 (chunk 43, "Management Role … management by fact") is the passage the expected answer paraphrases
Q7 3 → out loss: chunk 982 (both Type A/B definitions) replaced by 983 (Type A section) and 986 (combining A and B)
Q1 3 → 3 top-1 changed to chunk 32 ("Several key characteristics directly influenced the development of the model qualification methods") — the passage the expected answer is written from
Q4, Q10 not in top 10 the ceiling: no reranker can recover an answer that retrieval never returned

A limit of single-span evaluation. Each query has one marked answer span, but some answers are spread over several passages. For Q1 and Q9 the cross-encoder promoted chunks that genuinely answer the question yet do not contain our marked sentence, so hit@1 under-credits it. The spans were marked before the experiments and are kept fixed so that all methods are scored the same way; in Part D the LLM judge compares answers with the expected answer directly, which does not depend on spans.

C4. Did reranking help? (1 mark)¶

By the hit-rate metric, reranking did not help in our domain: hit@1 stayed at 20% and hit@3 at 60%, while each query paid about 52 ms extra — about 3.7× the cost of the hybrid search itself (14 ms), though still small next to the seconds an LLM needs to generate an answer. It changed the first result for 4 of 10 queries, and gains (Q6 to rank 1, Q2 into the top 3) were cancelled by losses (Q9, Q7). Inspection shows the metric understates it — for Q1 and Q9 the reranker promoted the passages the expected answers were written from — so we keep it for Part D, where the quality of the 3 chunks given to the model matters more than 52 ms.

import gc
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig
from peft import PeftModel

assert torch.cuda.is_available(), "Part D needs a GPU runtime (Runtime > Change runtime type > T4 GPU)"

# T4 (compute capability 7.5) has no native bfloat16, so compute in float16 there
COMPUTE_DTYPE = torch.bfloat16 if torch.cuda.get_device_capability()[0] >= 8 else torch.float16
BNB_4BIT = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
                              bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=COMPUTE_DTYPE, bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True)

ADAPTER_CANDIDATES = [Path("/content/drive/MyDrive/qlora_adapter_b_final"), Path("/content/qlora_adapter_b_final"),
                      Path("/home/jovyan/adapters/qlora_adapter_b_final"), Path("qlora_adapter_b_final")]
ADAPTER_PATH = next((p for p in ADAPTER_CANDIDATES if (p / "adapter_config.json").exists()), None)
assert ADAPTER_PATH, "Adapter not found: copy qlora_adapter_b_final/ from Assignment 1 into MyDrive/"
print("Compute dtype:", COMPUTE_DTYPE, "| Adapter:", ADAPTER_PATH)

def load_4bit(model_id):
    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
    if tok.pad_token is None:
        tok.pad_token = tok.eos_token
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, quantization_config=BNB_4BIT,
                                                 dtype=COMPUTE_DTYPE, device_map="auto")
    return model.eval(), tok

def chat_generate(model, tok, messages, max_new_tokens, **gen_kwargs):
    # Greedy decoding (do_sample=False == temperature 0): the same input always gives the same output.
    prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
    inputs = tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)
    with torch.no_grad():
        out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens, do_sample=False,
                             pad_token_id=tok.pad_token_id, **gen_kwargs)
    n_in = inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]
    return tok.decode(out[0][n_in:], skip_special_tokens=True).strip(), n_in

def free_gpu(*names):
    for n in names:
        globals().pop(n, None)
    gc.collect()
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    print(f"GPU memory in use: {torch.cuda.memory_allocated() / 1e9:.2f} GB")

D1. Generate grounded answers (3 marks)¶

D1.1 — The generation prompt (1 mark)¶

The rules go in the user message, because Adapter B was fine-tuned on user → assistant turns with no system prompt. Each chunk is numbered and labelled with its source document, so the model can cite [n].

In [35]:
NOT_FOUND = "Not found in the documents"

RAG_INSTRUCTIONS = f"""You are a manufacturing and technical-standards assistant.
Answer the question using ONLY the information in the numbered chunks below.
Rules:
1. Use only facts stated in the chunks. Do not use outside knowledge.
2. After each sentence, cite the chunk number(s) it came from in square brackets, for example [2] or [1][3].
3. If the chunks do not contain the answer, reply exactly: {NOT_FOUND}
4. Answer in at most 5 sentences."""

def build_prompt(question, chunks):
    blocks = "\n\n".join(f"[{i}] (source: {c['doc']})\n{c['text']}" for i, c in enumerate(chunks, start=1))
    return f"{RAG_INSTRUCTIONS}\n\nChunks:\n{blocks}\n\nQuestion: {question}\nAnswer (with chunk citations):"

print(build_prompt("<question>", [{"doc": "<source file>", "text": "<chunk text>"} for _ in range(3)]))

You are a manufacturing and technical-standards assistant.
Answer the question using ONLY the information in the numbered chunks below.
Rules:
1. Use only facts stated in the chunks. Do not use outside knowledge.
2. After each sentence, cite the chunk number(s) it came from in square brackets, for example [2] or [1][3].
3. If the chunks do not contain the answer, reply exactly: Not found in the documents
4. Answer in at most 5 sentences.

Chunks:
[1] (source: <source file>)
<chunk text>

[2] (source: <source file>)
<chunk text>

[3] (source: <source file>)
<chunk text>

Question: <question>
Answer (with chunk citations):

Fitting TinyLlama's 2,048-token window. Part A showed the top-3 chunks average ~1,440 TinyLlama tokens but can reach ~1,830. fit_chunks() measures the full prompt with the generator's own tokenizer and, only when prompt + 200 answer tokens would not fit, cuts the longest chunk(s) from the end until it does. Models with long windows are never trimmed.

In [36]:
MAX_NEW_TOKENS = 200

def fit_chunks(question, chunks, tok, context_limit):
    def prompt_len(cs):
        msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": build_prompt(question, cs)}]
        return len(tok(tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True))["input_ids"])

    ids = [tok(c["text"], add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"] for c in chunks]
    overhead  = prompt_len([{**c, "text": ""} for c in chunks])
    available = context_limit - MAX_NEW_TOKENS - overhead - 16          # 16 = safety margin for re-tokenisation
    cap = max(len(x) for x in ids)
    while sum(min(len(x), cap) for x in ids) > available:
        cap -= 8
    return [{**c, "text": tok.decode(x[:cap]) if len(x) > cap else c["text"], "trimmed": len(x) > cap}
            for c, x in zip(chunks, ids)]

The extra "not in the corpus" query (D1.3)¶

The corpus never mentions IATF 16949 or PPAP (checked below). This is a deliberately tempting question: it sounds like it belongs in the domain, and Assignment 1's training data mentioned IATF 16949, so a model that ignores the chunks may answer from memory. It goes through the same hybrid → rerank pipeline as the other queries.

D1.2 — Answers from the Assignment 1 model (1 mark)¶

In [38]:
def answer_all(model, tok, context_limit, **gen_kwargs):
    rows = []
    for e in GEN_CASES:
        chunks = fit_chunks(e["query"], FINAL_TOP3[e["qid"]], tok, context_limit)
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        answer, n_in = chat_generate(model, tok, [{"role": "user", "content": build_prompt(e["query"], chunks)}],
                                     MAX_NEW_TOKENS, **gen_kwargs)
        rows.append({"qid": e["qid"], "query": e["query"], "answer": answer, "chunks": chunks,
                     "prompt tokens": n_in, "trimmed": any(c["trimmed"] for c in chunks),
                     "cites chunks": bool(re.search(r"\[\d\]", answer)),
                     "says Not found": NOT_FOUND.lower() in answer.lower(),
                     "time (s)": round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 1)})
    return rows

def print_answers(rows, title):
    print(f"=== {title} ===\n")
    for r in rows:
        tag = " [NOT-IN-CORPUS QUERY]" if r["qid"] == NF_CASE["qid"] else ""
        print(f"Q{r['qid']}{tag}: {r['query']}")
        print(textwrap.indent(textwrap.fill(r["answer"], 110), "   "), "\n")

Q1: How did Malcolm Baldrige quality concepts influence the STEP model qualification approach?
   The Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award emphasized the importance of continuous improvement, management by
   fact, and the use of metrics in product development. The STEP qualification approach incorporates these
   principles into its approach to ensuring the quality of information models. The Baldrige approach was used as
   a guide for the STEP model qualification approach, which aimed to ensure the quality of information models by
   using quality management techniques such as continuous improvement, management by fact, and the use of
   metrics. 

Q2: How can workstation design reduce excessive reaching and awkward upper-body posture?
   The answer to the question "How can workstation design reduce excessive reaching and awkward upper-body
   posture?" is by using proper equipment and tools, such as powered dumpers, vacuum devices, and better
   conveyors to deliver products, reducing the need for reaching and increasing the use of straight wrists.
   Additionally, selecting a tool that has a curved or pistol-shaped handle, replacing this operation with an
   automatic pallet wrapper, and using multiple conveyors at different locations can also help reduce reaching
   and elevated arms. Finally, discussions about the posture of the left hand during sharpening and the use of
   circular saws should be avoided. 

Q3: What three kinds of evidence can be used to assess results under the Baldrige-inspired approach described in the report?
   The Baldrige-inspired approach described in the report uses three kinds of evidence to assess results: (1)
   improvement trends, (2) current levels, and (3) benchmarks, evaluations, and other comparisons that establish
   levels and trends relative to the performance of others, especially appropriately selected leaders. 

Q4: Why are statistical methods useful when analysing manufacturing experiments?
   Statistical methods are useful when analyzing manufacturing experiments because they provide a means of
   detecting and correcting for any potential sources of error in the experimental design, such as insufficiently
   large samples, inadequately controlled variables, or unmeasured confounding factors. By identifying and
   addressing these issues, statistical methods can help ensure the validity and reliability of the resulting
   data and conclusions. Additionally, statistical methods can also aid in interpreting and presenting the
   results of the experiments, providing insights into the underlying mechanisms and patterns that govern the
   observed data. 

Q5: What is the difference between reactive maintenance and more advanced maintenance strategies?
   The difference between reactive maintenance and more advanced maintenance strategies is that reactive
   maintenance does not involve any advanced maintenance techniques, while more advanced maintenance techniques
   involve advanced maintenance capabilities based on R&D activities or emerging, commercially available
   solutions. 

Q6: What costs are included when analysing direct and indirect machinery-maintenance impacts?

Q7: What is the difference between Type A and Type B evaluations of uncertainty?
   The difference between Type A and Type B evaluations of uncertainty is that Type A evaluations involve
   estimating the standard deviation of a measurement result, while Type B evaluations involve estimating the
   combined standard uncertainty of a measurement result, which includes individual standard deviations and
   covariances as well as the estimated standard deviation. 

Q8: What common elements are included in the ISO 9001, ISO 9002, and ISO 9003 quality-system models?
   The common elements included in the ISO 9001, ISO 9002, and ISO 9003 quality-system models are:  1. An
   effective quality system 2. Ensuring that measurements are valid, that measuring and testing equipment is

   guidelines for the application of ISO 9001 to the development, supply, and 

Q9: Why is management involvement important in a quality-improvement program?
   Management involvement is important in a quality-improvement program because it provides visibility to the
   results of quality assessments, allows for structural components to be identified, and breaks complex problems
   into recognizable components for managing product development. This structure promotes "management by fact"
   and enables the development of models with measurable targets for quality well in advance. 

Q10: What is the main purpose of machine guarding?

Q7: What is the difference between Type A and Type B evaluations of uncertainty?
   Type A evaluations of uncertainty are based on valid statistical methods for treating data, such as
   calculating the standard deviation of the mean of a series of independent observations [1], using the method
   of least squares to fit a curve to data in order to estimate the parameters of the curve and their standard
   deviations, and carrying out an analysis of variance (ANOVA) [1]. On the other hand, Type B evaluations are
   usually based on scientific judgment using all the relevant information available, which may include previous
   measurement data, experience with, or general knowledge of, the behavior and property of relevant materials
   and instruments, manufacturer’s specifications, data provided in calibration and other reports, and
   uncertainties assigned to reference data taken from handbooks [2]. Essentially, Type A relies on statistical
   data analysis, while Type B relies on expert judgment and available information.  References: [1]
   NIST_Measurement_Uncertainty.

Observations on the generated answers (D1.2)

  • Assignment 1 model (TinyLlama-1.1B + Adapter B): the problem that triggered the switch. None of its 10 answers cites a chunk, and for the not-in-corpus question it presents the EU conformity-assessment modules from the retrieved ISO 9000 chunks as "PPAP documents" instead of saying "Not found". Some answers also drift (Q6 lists survey question numbers instead of cost types). Fine-tuning taught it the domain's style and to always answer; it never saw citations or refusals, and a 1.1B model follows a 4-rule instruction poorly.
  • Phi-3.5-mini-instruct (final generator) stays on the chunks, cites chunk numbers in 9/10 answers and refuses the not-in-corpus question. The one miss is Q2, which cites slide numbers such as [46] instead (the \[\d\] regex only matches single-digit chunk numbers). Remaining weaknesses:
    • Citation accuracy: Q1 cites [4] although only 3 chunks were given; Q2 cites slide numbers; Q5 attributes the reactive-maintenance definition to [2] when it is in chunk [1].
    • Verbosity: it adds unrequested "References:" lists, and six answers (Q1, Q2, Q4–Q7) hit the 200-token limit, mostly while writing those lists. Q4 and Q5 are cut mid-sentence.
    • Q2 appends a contradictory "Not found in the documents: …" after a correct answer, so the string flag says Not found is True there. String flags are only a rough check; the LLM judge below reads the whole answer.

Correctly refused: True

Result. The answer ends with "Not found in the documents" and admits "the specific documents required for PPAP approval are not explicitly stated in the provided chunks", so the model does recognise that the corpus does not answer the question. It is not a clean refusal, though: its first sentence ("a supplier must submit a Quality Management System (QMS) registration document") is invented, since PPAP and IATF 16949 appear 0 times in the corpus. The retrieved chunks are about ISO 9000 registration and quality audits, and the model stitched a plausible-sounding claim from them before falling back. A stricter rule, such as "if the answer is not in the chunks, reply with that sentence alone and nothing else", would remove the invented preamble. TinyLlama, by contrast, answered this question at length with no refusal (example in the switch cell above).

D2. Check the answers with an LLM judge (4 marks)¶

D2.1 — Judge prompt and results (1 mark)¶

Judge model: Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (4-bit NF4, greedy decoding = temperature 0). It sees exactly what the generator saw (the same, possibly trimmed, 3 chunks) plus the question, the expected answer and the generated answer. The two checks are kept separate on purpose: an answer can be correct but unsupported (true, but from the model's memory) or supported but wrong (faithful to chunks that do not answer the question) — these point to different fixes.

In [42]:
JUDGE_MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct"

JUDGE_SYSTEM = ("You are a strict examiner grading answers produced by a question-answering system. "
                "Follow the marking scheme exactly and reply only in the required format.")

JUDGE_TEMPLATE = """You will check ONE answer on TWO separate criteria.

QUESTION:
{question}

EXPECTED ANSWER (reference answer from the evaluation set):
{expected}

RETRIEVED CHUNKS (the only material the system was allowed to use):
{chunks}

SYSTEM ANSWER:
{answer}

CHECK 1 - CORRECT: compare the SYSTEM ANSWER with the EXPECTED ANSWER only (ignore the chunks for this check).
- CORRECT: states the main point(s) of the expected answer and contradicts nothing in it. Wording may differ; missing minor details is fine.
- PARTLY_CORRECT: gets at least one main point right, but misses other main points or includes a claim that conflicts with the expected answer.
- WRONG: misses the main point, contradicts the expected answer, is off-topic, or replies "Not found in the documents".

CHECK 2 - SUPPORTED: compare the SYSTEM ANSWER with the RETRIEVED CHUNKS only (ignore the expected answer for this check).
- YES: every factual statement in the answer is stated in, or directly follows from, the chunks. Citation numbers and formatting do not matter.
- NO: at least one statement is not in the chunks (outside knowledge or invention), even if it is true.
- A reply of "Not found in the documents" makes no factual claims, so it is SUPPORTED: YES.

Reply with exactly these four lines and nothing else:
CORRECT: <CORRECT or PARTLY_CORRECT or WRONG>
SUPPORTED: <YES or NO>
REASON: <one sentence explaining both verdicts>
UNSUPPORTED: <the first unsupported statement quoted word for word, or NONE>"""

def judge_messages(e, row):
    chunks = "\n\n".join(f"[{i}] {c['text']}" for i, c in enumerate(row["chunks"], start=1))
    return [{"role": "system", "content": JUDGE_SYSTEM},
            {"role": "user", "content": JUDGE_TEMPLATE.format(question=e["query"], expected=e["expected"],
                                                              chunks=chunks, answer=row["answer"])}]

def parse_verdict(text):
    grab = lambda pattern: (m.group(1).strip() if (m := re.search(pattern, text, re.I | re.M)) else None)
    correct = grab(r"^\s*CORRECT:\s*(PARTLY[ _]CORRECT|CORRECT|WRONG)")
    return {"correct": correct.upper().replace(" ", "_") if correct else "PARSE_ERROR",
            "supported": (grab(r"^\s*SUPPORTED:\s*(YES|NO)") or "PARSE_ERROR").upper(),
            "reason": grab(r"^\s*REASON:\s*(.+)$") or "",
            "unsupported": grab(r"^\s*UNSUPPORTED:\s*(.+)$") or ""}

print(JUDGE_TEMPLATE)

- PARTLY_CORRECT: gets at least one main point right, but misses other main points or includes a claim that conflicts with the expected answer.
- WRONG: misses the main point, contradicts the expected answer, is off-topic, or replies "Not found in the documents".

CHECK 2 - SUPPORTED: compare the SYSTEM ANSWER with the RETRIEVED CHUNKS only (ignore the expected answer for this check).
- YES: every factual statement in the answer is stated in, or directly follows from, the chunks. Citation numbers and formatting do not matter.
- NO: at least one statement is not in the chunks (outside knowledge or invention), even if it is true.
- A reply of "Not found in the documents" makes no factual claims, so it is SUPPORTED: YES.

Reply with exactly these four lines and nothing else:
CORRECT: <CORRECT or PARTLY_CORRECT or WRONG>
SUPPORTED: <YES or NO>
REASON: <one sentence explaining both verdicts>
UNSUPPORTED: <the first unsupported statement quoted word for word, or NONE>

Reading the summary. The judge passed all 10 answers on both checks. That is more generous than a careful reader (see the spot-check in D2.2): a 7B judge given the rule "missing minor details is fine" tends to accept answers that share the expected answer's vocabulary. Also, by design our SUPPORTED check ignores citation numbers, so wrong citations (Q1's non-existent [4], Q2's slide numbers) do not count against an answer. So treat 10/10 as an upper bound, not as proof that every answer is right.

D2.2 — Spot-check the judge (1 mark)¶

show_case(qid) prints everything the judge saw, so you can grade the answer yourself first and then compare.

def show_case(qid, width=110):
    e, g, j = EVAL[qid - 1], gen_by_qid[qid], judge_df.set_index("qid").loc[qid]
    print(f"Q{qid}: {e['query']}\n\nEXPECTED: {textwrap.fill(e['expected'], width)}\n")
    for i, c in enumerate(g["chunks"], start=1):
        print(f"[{i}] ({c['doc']}, chunk {c['chunk_id']}{', trimmed' if c['trimmed'] else ''})")
        print(textwrap.indent(textwrap.fill(c["text"], width), "    "), "\n")
    print(f"ANSWER: {textwrap.fill(g['answer'], width)}\n")
    print(f"JUDGE : CORRECT={j.correct} | SUPPORTED={j.supported}\n        {j.reason}\n        unsupported: {j.unsupported}")

show_case(1)

D2.2 answer — our spot-check of Q1, Q2 and Q4¶

We read each answer with its 3 chunks and decided our own verdict before looking at the judge's.

Query Our verdict Judge's verdict Agree?
Q1 Baldrige concepts → STEP qualification CORRECT, SUPPORTED CORRECT, YES ✅ both
Q2 workstation design vs reaching/posture CORRECT, SUPPORTED CORRECT, YES ✅ both
Q4 statistical methods in experiments PARTLY_CORRECT, SUPPORTED CORRECT, YES ❌ correct · ✅ supported

We agree with 5 of the 6 verdicts (2 of the 3 answers fully).

  • Q1 (shown above): continuous improvement, management by fact, metrics, linking processes to results and benchmarks are all in chunks [1] and [3], and they cover most of the expected answer. One flaw the judge does not see: the answer cites [4], but only 3 chunks were given. Our SUPPORTED rule deliberately ignores citation numbers, so this is not penalised.
  • Q2: diverters, cut-outs/chutes, properly adjusted platforms and pistol-grip handles all come from chunk [2] (#1174: "This conveyor has diverters in place that push the products closer to the workers. This reduces reaches…", "Poorly adjusted platforms can be responsible for hand/wrists deviations, elevated upper arms") and match the three examples in the expected answer. Its flaws are formatting: it cites slide numbers [46]–[49] instead of chunk numbers and ends with a stray "Not found in the documents" sentence.
  • Disagreement, Q4: the expected answer is about experiments: summarising observations, describing variation, and judging whether an apparent difference is meaningful. The system answer is about Statistical Process Control monitoring production (chunk [1]). It shares the idea of variation but never explains how statistics decide whether an experimental difference is real, so we rate it PARTLY_CORRECT. The judge probably matched on shared vocabulary ("statistical methods", "variation") and stretched the rubric's "missing minor details is fine" to cover a missing main point. Its SUPPORTED: YES is right: every statement is in chunk [1].

Takeaway: the judge is lenient on correctness, so the 10/10 above is an upper bound. A stricter judge prompt would list the expected answer's key points and ask for each one to be ticked off before giving a label.

D2.3 — Find the cause of one failure (1 mark)¶

For a failed answer, the key question is was the needed information in the 3 chunks?

  • No → retrieval problem (chunking, search or reranking did not surface it).
  • Yes → generation problem (the model ignored, misread or embellished what it was given).

diagnose(qid) gives a first signal — whether the marked answer span is in the chunks — but, as Part C showed, an answer can also be present in a chunk without our exact span, so always read the chunks (show_case) before deciding.

In [46]:
def diagnose(qid):
    e, g, j = EVAL[qid - 1], gen_by_qid[qid], judge_df.set_index("qid").loc[qid]
    span_in = [i for i, c in enumerate(g["chunks"], start=1) if is_hit(c["text"], e["span"])]
    print(f"Q{qid}: judge says CORRECT={j.correct}, SUPPORTED={j.supported}")
    print(f"Answer span present in chunk(s): {span_in or 'none'}"
          f" -> first signal: {'GENERATION problem' if span_in else 'RETRIEVAL problem (confirm by reading the chunks)'}")
    print(f"Hybrid rank of the answer span before reranking: {first_hit_rank(candidates[qid], e['span']) or 'not in top 10'}")

failed = judge_df.query("correct != 'CORRECT' or supported == 'NO'").qid.tolist()
print("Failed or unsupported answers:", failed)
for q in failed:
    diagnose(q); print()

Was the needed information in the chunks? Mostly no, so retrieval caused the problem.

  • The passage that answers the question, Handbook ch. 3: "One of the most frequent uses of statistics is in testing for differences … apply a statistical test to the experimental results to see whether we would be justified in concluding that there is a difference", is in none of the 3 chunks and not even in the hybrid top 10 (Part C: Q4 is one of the two queries out of the reranker's reach).
  • What was retrieved is off-target: chunk [1] is about SPC monitoring a running process (from a different document, the QIF report), chunk [2] is a reference list plus a table-of-contents paragraph, and chunk [3] introduces descriptive vs inductive statistics.
  • Generation played only a small part: chunk [3] does say "Descriptive statistical methods are those which are used to summarize or describe data", which matches one point of the expected answer, but the model built its answer around chunk [1]. Even a perfect generator could not state the main point, judging whether a difference is real, from these chunks.

Why retrieval missed it: in the handbook the answer sentence follows tolerance-limit tables, a reference list and a chapter heading, so the 400-token chunk that contains it mixes unrelated material and its embedding is diluted. Chunk [1], meanwhile, repeats the query's words ("statistical methods", "manufacturing", "variation") many times.

D2.4 — Suggest a fix (1 mark)¶

Fix: small-to-big ("parent chunk") retrieval — search over 100-token chunks, but give the generator the surrounding ~400-token passage.

  • Why it fixes Q4. The failure is in ranking long, mixed-topic chunks, and Part A already shows the small-chunk side works: with 100-token chunks dense search found Q4's answer span at rank 3, while with 400-token chunks it fell outside the top 3 (Part A) and outside the top 5 for every method (Part B). A 100-token chunk that begins "One of the most frequent uses of statistics is in testing for differences" has an embedding dominated by that idea, so it matches a question about why statistics are used to analyse experiments.
  • Why not simply switch to 100-token chunks. They split the Q2 and Q5 spans and give the model too little context for multi-part answers (A2.2). Mapping each small hit back to its parent passage keeps the sharp matching of small chunks and the context of large ones; the cross-encoder then reranks the parents, and the prompt still carries 3 × ~400 tokens, so it fits the same budget.
  • How we would check it. Re-run the Part B/C hit rates and the Q4 judge verdict. Adding ~100 tokens of overlap between chunks would also stop answer spans from being cut at chunk boundaries.
